title: What should you say when the interviewer hands you a chart?
description: Exhibits test whether you can find what matters, and many cases turn on them. What to do, what to say, and the mistake to avoid.
hook: When the interviewer hands you a chart, ask for a moment, read the title, axes, units and footnotes, and then lead with the insight, not a description: what stands out, how big it is in numbers, and what it means for the client's goal. Finish by proposing what you would look at next. Most of the marks are in the so-what, not in reading the bars.
body:
Stage 6 of 10 in the ten stages of a case.

Why charts matter

Most cases include at least one exhibit: a chart, a table or a small P&L. Exhibits test whether you can find what matters in a mass of data, and many cases turn on a single number hidden in one. The common mistake is describing the chart ("this shows sales by region over three years") instead of saying what it means.

A 30-second routine

Ask for a moment first. It is expected, and it prevents most chart mistakes.

"Thank you. May I take a moment to read this?"

Then, in order:

  1. Read the title. It tells you what the chart is about and sometimes the time period.
  2. Read the axes and units. Revenue or volume? Dollars or percentages? Thousands or millions?
  3. Read the footnotes and legend. The detail that changes everything often hides here.
  4. Find the biggest change or the odd one out. Then size it with a quick calculation.
  5. Write two insights before you speak, and decide which matters more for the goal.

Insights, not description

A good chart answer does four things: it says what stands out, quantifies it, links it to the goal and proposes a next step. Do the maths without being asked. If the interviewer has to ask "and how big is that?", they have done part of your job for you.

A worked example

A retailer's total sales fell from $100M to $92M in a year. The chart shows sales by region:

RegionLast yearThis yearChange
North$40M$30M−$10M
South$35M$36M+$1M
West$25M$26M+$1M
Total$100M$92M−$8M
Weak: "The North went down, and the South and West went up a bit."
Strong: "Two things stand out. First, the North fell $10M, a quarter of its sales, which is more than the whole $8M decline. Second, the other two regions actually grew by $2M between them. So this is a North problem, not a company-wide one. Next I'd like to understand what changed there: a lost customer, store closures or a new competitor. Do we have North sales by store?"

The strong answer quantifies (−$10M, a quarter), connects parts of the chart (North versus the rest), states the implication and asks for the next piece of data.

Percentages versus dollars

Watch for charts that invite you to confuse growth rates with impact. If product A grows 50% from $2M, it adds $1M. If product B grows 10% from $30M, it adds $3M. A is growing faster, but B contributes three times as much new revenue. Always ask what the bars measure, revenue, volume, share or margin, because the labels decide what you can conclude.

If you are stuck or wrong

Say it out loud. Silence reads as panic; a structured step back reads as composure.

"I'd like to take a step back and re-read this. We know A, B and C, and we're trying to get to X."

If you realise you misread a unit, correct it plainly: "Sorry, I read that as thousands; it's millions, so the gap is $3M, not $3,000." A calm, quick correction costs you very little.

Common mistakes

  • Describing the chart. Lead with what it means.
  • Skipping the units and footnotes. The most expensive misreads come from here.
  • Reporting percentages without dollars. Size the impact.
  • Listing five observations. Pick the two that matter most and rank them.
  • Stopping at the insight. End with a next step and a data request.

Practise the moment

Say your answer out loud before you open the model.

1. The interviewer hands you a dense chart. What do you say?

Show a strong answer

"Thank you. May I take a moment to read this?" Then read the title, axes, units and footnotes before saying anything else.

Why it works: Thirty seconds of reading prevents the usual chart mistakes.

2. A chart shows recycled plastic demand overtaking supply from 2028, with a gap of 20% by 2030. Your client must use recycled plastic by law from 2030. Start your answer.

Show a strong answer

"Two things stand out. First, supply is fine until 2027, but demand overtakes it from 2028. Second, by 2030 the market is 20% short, just as our client legally needs the material. So supply is a real risk, and prices will likely rise. Next I'd like to know how much our client needs and how it could secure it."

Why it works: Insights with numbers, prioritised, linked to the client and ending with a next step. This exhibit is from the PackRight case.

3. A chart shows a client's market share fell from 25% to 20% while the market grew from $400M to $600M. Is the client shrinking?

Show a strong answer

"No. Revenue grew from 25% × $400M = $100M to 20% × $600M = $120M, up 20%. But the market grew 50%, so we are losing ground to competitors. I'd like to see which competitors gained share and in which segments."

Why it works: It checks the dollars behind the percentages before drawing a conclusion.

Where to practise next

Use the chart drill for quick reps, and browse the graph library to see every chart type you are likely to meet. For the full method, read how to read a chart and find the insight, then the next stage, getting through the maths without mistakes.
